title: How the Kessmouth market reached the quay
question: How did the Kessmouth market end up on the quay, and which decision made it happen?

sources.title: The harbour bell of Kessmouth
sources.text:
# The harbour bell of Kessmouth

An original, fictional account written for Break the Wall. Kessmouth and its people are invented.

In the spring of 1871 a storm broke the harbour wall of Kessmouth.
Two boats sank at their moorings, and the fishermen blamed the wall, not the storm.
The council could afford one repair: the wall or the old market hall.
The harbour master, Ada Pell, argued for the wall, because without boats there would be nothing to sell.
The merchants argued for the hall, because their stalls stood in the rain.
Ada Pell won the vote by one voice, after she promised to ring the harbour bell whenever a storm was coming.

The wall was rebuilt over the summer with stone from the closed quarry at Hale.
Reopening the quarry brought twenty workers to the town, and they needed somewhere to eat.
With no market hall, the merchants moved their stalls to the quay beside the new wall.
The quay was busier than the hall had ever been, because every boat now landed its catch there.

In October the bell rang for the first storm of the season.
The boats came in early, and the merchants carried their stalls back from the quay.
Nothing was lost, and the council ordered the bell to be rung before every storm from then on.

By 1875 the old market hall had become a storehouse, and nobody asked to repair it again.
The town remembers Ada Pell for the wall; the merchants remember her for the quay.

Historians of the town disagree about the quay.
Some say the market would have moved anyway, once the railway reached the harbour in 1874.
Others point out that the stalls were already on the quay three years before the railway came.

whole.name: From storm to quay
whole.does: Follows one vote after a storm through its consequences, until the market sits on the quay and the old hall is forgotten.
whole.why: Nobody decided to move the market. It moved because a vote spent the only repair on the wall, and the quay filled the gap.

parts.name: The storm breaks the wall
parts.role: The event that forces a choice.

points.text: A spring storm breaks the harbour wall and two boats sink.
The fishermen blame the wall, not the storm.

parts.name: One repair, one vote
parts.role: The council can repair the wall or the market hall, not both.

points.text: Only one repair is affordable: the wall or the hall.
Ada Pell wins by one voice, after promising the storm bell.

parts.name: Ada Pell, for the wall
parts.explain: Without boats there would be nothing to sell, so the wall comes first.

parts.name: The merchants, for the hall
parts.explain: Their stalls stood in the rain, so they wanted the hall repaired.

parts.name: The bell promise
parts.role: The concession that wins the vote.
parts.explain: Ada Pell promises to ring the harbour bell before every storm, and wins by one voice.

parts.name: The wall is rebuilt
parts.role: The repair that was chosen, and its side effect.

points.text: The wall is rebuilt with stone from the reopened quarry.
Twenty quarry workers arrive and need somewhere to eat.

parts.name: The bell proves itself
parts.role: The promise is kept at the first storm.

points.text: The bell rings before the first October storm.
Boats and stalls are moved in time, and nothing is lost.

parts.name: The market moves to the quay

points.text: With no hall, the merchants set up on the quay beside the new wall.
The quay is busier than the hall, because every boat lands there.

parts.name: The hall is forgotten
parts.role: What the vote cost, years later.

points.text: By 1875 the hall is a storehouse and nobody asks to repair it.
The town remembers the wall; the merchants remember the quay.
Some historians say the railway of 1874 would have moved the market anyway.
But the stalls were on the quay three years earlier.

excluded.note: Title and the note that the account is invented.

runs.title: Remove an event
runs.question: Which event, if it had not happened, would keep the market off the quay?

bricks.explain: It falls. Spending the repair on the wall is what left the merchants without a hall.
It weakens. The market still moves, but without the warning a storm could have ruined the stalls. The text does not say what would have happened.
It holds. The stalls were on the quay three years before the railway arrived.

runs.title: Apply it to a new case
runs.scenario: In a nearby town a fire destroys the market hall, and the council rebuilds it at once.
runs.question: Following the Kessmouth account, would that market move to the quay?

options.text: Yes: markets always move towards the boats
options.why: Kessmouth's market moved because it had no hall, not because of a general rule.

options.text: Probably not: the hall it relied on is still there
options.why: In Kessmouth the move filled a gap left by the vote. Here there is no gap.

reassemble.title: Rebuild the chain of events
reassemble.instruction: Put each event in its place, from the storm to the forgotten hall, and set the rival cause aside.

hints.vote: A choice had to be made before any repair.
hints.bell: This was the price of winning the vote.
hints.quay: It happened because something was missing.
hints.hall: Years later, this is what the vote cost.
hints.railway: It came after the move it is said to explain.
